text: <blocked>bad() declares `char *data;` and immediately passes it, still uninitialized, to printLine(data). printLine only guards against a NULL line, so unless that indeterminate stack value happens to equal exactly 0 - which nothing in bad()'s parameterless signature lets a caller force or control - printLine will dereference that wild pointer via printf("%s\n", line), reading arbitrary memory until it happens to hit a NUL byte. This is undefined behavior (use of an indeterminate value feeding a likely invalid memory read) built into bad() itself: it is non-deterministic (the exact garbage address, and whether the run crashes, depends on whatever was previously on the stack, which differs across compilers, optimization levels, and runs) and would be flagged by AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. Because bad is a mandatory listed symbol that must be called directly and is also reached through driver(0), and it takes no arguments through which a caller could make the call safe, no driver satisfying the "never trigger undefined behavior / sanitizer-clean / deterministic output" requirements can be written for this unit.</blocked>
